references.text: Jesus repeats this motif on the way to the cross: "Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days!" – [ref:Luk 23:29|Luke 23:29] shows Jesus' lament over the women of Jerusalem and their coming suffering.
Hosea speaks of woe upon Israel when God turns away from them – [ref:Hos 9:12|Hosea 9:12] specifically mentions woe to those who lose their children, an image of the coming judgment.
[ref:5 Mos 28:53-57|Deuteronomy 28:53–57] describes the terrible conditions during a siege, where pregnant and nursing women suffer most, which was fulfilled at the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.

The parallel passage in Matthew's version of the end-times discourse: [ref:Matt 24:19-21|Matthew 24:19–21] contains the same statement about woe to the pregnant and nursing, as well as mention of the great tribulation.

The parallel passage in Mark's version: [ref:Mark 13:17-19|Mark 13:17–19] has the same cry of woe over those who are pregnant and nursing in those days, followed by a description of the great distress.
[ref:Klag 4:10|Lamentations 4:10] describes the cruel reality during Jerusalem's destruction, where mothers cooked their own children – a fulfillment of the words of the curse.
Paul speaks of God's wrath (ὀργή) that has come upon the Jews – [ref:1 Tess 2:16|1 Thessalonians 2:16] uses the same term for God's wrath against the people, in agreement with Jesus' prophecy.

[ref:5 Mos 28:15|Deuteronomy 28:15] introduces the curses that come upon the people through disobedience – the background for the expressions "ἀνάγκη μεγάλη" (great distress) and "ὀργὴ τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ" (wrath against this people).
[ref:Dan 9:26|Daniel 9:26] prophesies the destruction of the city and sanctuary, with flood and war – a prophecy about the great distress that would come upon Jerusalem and the people.
[ref:Sef 1:15|Zephaniah 1:15] describes the day of the Lord as a day of distress and trouble (ἀνάγκη), an expression reflected in Jesus' words about the great distress over the land.
[ref:Rom 2:5|Romans 2:5] speaks of storing up wrath (ὀργή) for the day of wrath – the same theme of God's wrath against the people who are guilty of disobedience.
